content: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg)-positive patients were more frequently referred to specialists in the non-reflex testing group compared to the reflex testing group. However, the 95% confidence intervals for these proportions overlapped between the two groups. Among the HBsAg-positive individuals, 3% had detectable hepatitis B virus (HBV) DNA, and 2% were referred to HBV specialists for further evaluation of treatment eligibility. Of these, 0% initiated hepatitis B treatment. The quality of evidence supporting these findings was rated as very low. Reflex testing, which involves immediate one-step testing, demonstrated a turnaround time of 0 days from HBsAg testing to reflex sample collection. One study reported that the time from viral load (VL) testing to results availability was 105 minutes, and the time from results availability to treatment initiation was 40 minutes. Overall, the total turnaround time from HBsAg-positive screening to treatment initiation was approximately three hours and 25 minutes. Reflex testing for HBV DNA has the potential to reduce turnaround time, improve access to DNA testing, and expedite treatment initiation. These findings support the use of laboratory-based or clinic-based reflex viral load testing as an alternative to the standard multistep diagnostic strategy for HBV DNA quantification, facilitating linkage to care and treatment. Hepatitis D virus (HDV) is a defective RNA virus that requires co-infection with HBV for its replication and infectivity. Chronic hepatitis D is the most aggressive form of viral hepatitis, with rapid progression to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Globally, HDV affects approximately 5% of HBsAg-positive individuals, equating to 12 million people. Novel treatments, such as bulevirtide, have shown promising results and were approved by the European Medicines Agency in 2023. Historically, there has been limited guidance on HDV testing, and the World Health Organization (WHO) had no formal recommendations on who to test or how to test for HDV infection. The WHO developed a PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) question to guide recommendations on HDV testing among HBsAg-positive individuals. Evidence on the impact, cost, and cost-effectiveness of universal versus risk-based HDV antibody testing approaches was reviewed. Due to the limited number of studies meeting the PICO criteria, a systematic review was not feasible, and a narrative review was conducted instead. No studies directly evaluated the impact or cost-effectiveness of HDV testing strategies. However, evidence suggests that universal reflex HDV antibody testing significantly increases testing uptake and case detection compared to risk-based approaches. Universal HDV testing involves routine antibody testing for all HBsAg-positive individuals, regardless of risk factors or clinical characteristics. In contrast, focused (risk-based) testing targets specific high-risk populations, such as individuals from HDV-endemic regions, people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, sex workers, and those with advanced liver disease. Universal testing may improve case detection, treatment uptake, and epidemiological surveillance but requires enhanced laboratory infrastructure and resources. Risk-based testing may be more cost-effective in low-prevalence settings but relies on provider knowledge of HDV epidemiology and patient willingness to disclose risk factors. Challenges in HDV testing include low testing rates, limited access to diagnostics, and suboptimal performance of HDV RNA assays, particularly for certain genotypes. Reflex testing, which automatically triggers HDV antibody testing for HBsAg-positive individuals, has been shown to increase testing uptake and case detection. However, its implementation is limited by laboratory capacity and the availability of standardized HDV assays. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for HDV antibodies are not yet commercially available, further limiting decentralized testing options. Future research priorities include generating high-quality epidemiological data, evaluating the cost-effectiveness and feasibility of universal testing in lowand middle-income countries, validating HDV diagnostic assays, and developing rapid diagnostic tests to facilitate decentralized care. Additionally, fully automated nucleic acid tests (NATs) are needed to improve the accuracy and reliability of HDV RNA detection across all genotypes.
